# NRTH.dll — plaintexts recovered from the sample's own string decryptors
#
# sample        : NRTH.dll
# codec         : plain[p] = cipher[p] XOR ((p - K) & 0xFF); one-shot flag at record+F, L = F-1
# source of truth: working/recovered.json (tools/nrth_strings_recover.py, capstone)
# generated by  : recovered_or_reconstructed_project/tools/nrth_case_strings.py
#
# Meaning of the columns
#   VA        = address of the *call site* that decrypts the record (not of the data)
#   dec       = address of the decryptor function (one per record length)
#   key       = the per-decryptor constant K in  plain[p] = cipher[p] ^ ((p-K)&0xFF)
#   visibility: HIDDEN  = the plaintext does not appear anywhere in strings_catalog.txt,
#                         i.e. only the decoder reveals it (this is the useful half)
#             PLAIN+REC = also present as a plain string in the image
#
# No claim below is inferred from naming: each line is a byte-exact decode of bytes in
# the sample. Interpretations (why a string exists) are NOT included here; see
# mechanism_overview_ar.md and report.md for those, with their own confidence tags.

==============================================================================
SECTION A' — decodes that are NOT usable as indicators (17 records)
==============================================================================
Why they are separated: the sample builds several of these records at run time (the
ciphertext is fetched from a .data global by a helper such as 0x10023670, so the bytes
in the file image are not the final input) and for short records more than one key can
produce printable text. Listing them keeps the record count honest (82 decryptors /
63 records) while making clear that only Sections A and C are evidence.

==============================================================================
SECTION C — code signatures the tool searches for in other modules
==============================================================================
These are x86 pattern strings (with '?' wildcards) that NRTH.dll decrypts at runtime and
hands to its module scanner/resolver (0x10002960) to locate functions in client.dll /
netc.dll. They are *not* strings that belong to MTA itself, which is exactly what makes
them usable as memory-integrity anchors: find the function by the pattern, then look at
its first bytes (PRISTINE vs E9/FF 25/C3).

C.1 High confidence — recovered from a decryptor record, module + owner function known
    (20 entries; src/nrth_audit_sigs.h also compiles them into the audit module)

    the netc.dll patch cluster). These are the *targets of the 0xC3 writes*, i.e. the

==============================================================================
SECTION E — two run-time identifiers worth knowing about, verified outside the JSON
==============================================================================
  @custom       PLAIN string at .rdata file offset 0x000e9890 (VA 0x100ea890); it is
                already visible in strings_catalog.txt line 6091. Role (Lua chunk name
                for the menu's Execute path) is Strongly inferred from 0x10004550.
  @auto_inject  NOT present as a plain string. It is built from inline immediates on
                the stack at the auto-inject path near 0x100044df and decrypts with
                K=0x20; the ciphertext bytes and the decode are frozen as check 3 of
                NrthAuditSelfTest() (src/nrth_audit.cpp), so `nrth_audit selftest`
                re-verifies it on every run: 93 b5 a0 a2 b8 87 b0 b4 b1 b9 be aa.
  C:\NVX        a plain .rdata string (file offset 0x000afd18) that does NOT appear in
                any decryptor record. Earlier case text implied the config path came
                from an encrypted record — it does not: the config path the payload
                actually decrypts is C:\Overwack\loader_config.cfg (Section A).

==============================================================================
SECTION D — how to reproduce / how to use this file
==============================================================================
    cd recovered_or_reconstructed_project
    python3 tools/nrth_strings_recover.py ../working/NRTH.dll -o ../working/recovered.json
    python3 tools/nrth_sig_export.py      ../working/NRTH.dll -o ../working/sigs.json
    python3 tools/nrth_case_strings.py            # regenerates this file

Detection use:
  * Section A gives file/hash-independent strings for the *loader's* config path and for
    the ADS/cache locations — see detection/telemetry.md Layer 1.
  * Section C.1 is what NRTH_audit.dll scans with; the YARA rules in yara_rules.yar carry
    a subset of the same patterns for scan-time use (YARA cannot do the widen/patch logic).
  * Section C.2 must NOT be used as a cheat-presence indicator on its own: those prologue
    shapes are ordinary MSVC __SEH_prolog4 / __GS-setup code and appear in many modules.
    They are useful as *the location to check* once the cheat is known — the functions they name are the
    report channels (screenshot/transgression), so check their entry bytes in the LOADED image.

Verification:
  * Every address in this file is a VA (ImageBase + RVA) unless it is written `off 0x...`, which is a
    raw file offset in the packed image.  Re-check any claim mechanically:
        python3 tools/nrth_string_va.py ../working/NRTH.dll 'North Cheat'
        python3 tools/nrth_string_va.py ../working/NRTH.dll --check "0x100ea0d8=North Cheat"
        python3 tools/nrth_string_va.py ../working/NRTH.dll --audit-docs --also "../working/NORTH LOADER.exe" <docs...>
  * The regenerate paths above were fixed on 2026-10-11 (`../../working/` did not exist from that
    working directory; the sample lives in `working/` at the repository root).
